query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the phosphorus content by approximately 5 at% in a baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 high-entropy alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 high-entropy alloy produced via standard melt-spinning with an amorphous structure achieved only at extreme cooling rates.
generation.intervention: Incrementally raise the phosphorus concentration by ~5 atomic percent while keeping all other constituent concentrations constant.
generation.conditions: Applied during melting and rapid solidification under controlled inert-atmosphere conditions; expected to work under high cooling rates typical of melt-spinning but also permit slower quench conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Lowered liquidus temperature and formation of stable, phosphorus-rich clusters or phosphide-like short-range orders that suppress heterogeneous nucleation.
generation.mechanism: The extra phosphorus further broadens the solidification range and increases undercooling, thereby kinetically hindering crystallization and stabilizing the amorphous structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the critical cooling rate window for amorphization by an estimated 20–30% and a shift in the onset crystallization temperature upward by approximately 50 K relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The original Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy with established critical cooling rates and crystallization parameters.
generation.boundary: Excessive phosphorus beyond the optimum may lead to the formation of detrimental phosphide phases and embrittlement, thus the improvement is expected only within a moderate increase.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements depend on the interaction with other elements and may vary with processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one with the baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 composition and one with an increased phosphorus content by ~5 at%. Produce ribbons via melt-spinning under identical cooling conditions and characterize the resulting microstructure via X-ray diffraction and DSC.
measurements: XRD peak broadening indicative of amorphous structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the phosphorus-enhanced alloy fails to show a statistically significant (~20% improvement in glass-forming window or ~50 K increase in crystallization onset temperature) improvement over the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

In particular, the addition of phosphorus has been shown to significantly support amorphization processes, thereby promoting the formation of stable metallic glass structures [,].

The cooling profile recorded during welding (at a cooling rate of 154 K/s) demonstrates that the Cantor alloy solidifies at a temperature of 1478 K []. Previous studies reported its melting temperatures as 1607 K [,], 1523 K [], and 1543 K [], indicating a relatively narrow range of solidification. In contrast, the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy containing phosphorus exhibits a significantly broader solidification temperature range and more complex crystallization behavior. Pronounced thermal effects were observed at T3 = 1291 K and T4 = 1206 K during slow cooling on a copper plate (52 K/s), and at T3 = 977 K and T4 = 960 K during rapid cooling following a brief electric arc pulse (3018 K/s). This marked reduction in solidification temperatures compared to the Cantor alloy demonstrates the role of phosphorus in modifying thermal behavior and promoting amorphization. These results highlight the critical importance of controlling cooling rates and alloy composition to optimize phase stability and microstructure. In this paper, two new high entropy bulk metallic glasses (HE-BMGs) have been successfully fabricated using copper mold casting method, namely Ti20Hf20Cu20Ni20Be20 with a critical diameter of 2 mm and Ti16.7Zr16.7Nb16.7Cu16.7Ni16.7Be16.7 with a critical diameter of 1.5 mm. These two HE-BMGs exhibit high fracture strength over 2300 MPa. The glass forming ability and atomic size distribution characteristics of the HE-BMGs are discussed, and it is found that atomic radius spans over a wide range in HE-BMGs. Moreover, we propose a new parameter δ′ to assess the degree of lattice distortion in high entropy alloys (HEAs). It emphasizes the difference between atoms with adjacent atomic size, and it is closely related to phase selection in HEAs. When δ′ is relatively small (δ′ < 2.2), FCC solid solution formed; when 2.2 < δ′ < 2.9, FCC + BCC phases formed; when 2.9 < δ′ < 4.9, BCC phase formed; while δ′ > 4.9, amorphous phase would be formed. This new parameter δ′ is beneficial for understanding lattice distortion and phase selection in HEAs. papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.approach: Systematic variation of cooling rates (from slow cooling on a copper plate at 52 K/s to rapid cooling after an electric arc pulse at 3018 K/s) coupled with phase diagram analysis
papers.findings: Phosphorus broadens the solidification temperature range, lowers peak solidification temperatures, and promotes amorphization under extremely rapid cooling (e.g., melt-spun ribbons yield amorphous structures). Additional phases, such as phosphide-rich eutectics, are observed under specific cooling conditions.
papers.mechanism: Phosphorus modifies crystallization pathways by reducing the liquidus temperature of phosphorus‐poor primary phases and promoting the formation of phosphide phases, thus enhancing undercooling and suppressing nucleation of crystalline phases.

papers.title: Predictive Modeling of High-Entropy Alloys and Amorphous Metallic Alloys Using Machine Learning.
papers.system: Various multi-principal-element and amorphous metallic alloys (with discussion indirectly relevant to phosphorus effects)
papers.approach: Utilized models based on enthalpy of mixing, configurational entropy, and atomic radii mismatch to predict glass-forming ability
papers.findings: More negative mixing enthalpy and high configurational entropy correlate with higher glass-forming ability. Atomic size mismatch enhances viscosity in the liquid state, restricting atomic diffusion and favoring glass formation.
papers.mechanism: Increased disorder from entropy and local atomic size mismatch disrupts crystal nucleation, stabilizing the amorphous state.

papers.title: Designing High Entropy Bulk Metallic Glass (HE-BMG) by Similar Element Substitution/Addition.
papers.system: High-entropy bulk metallic glasses (e.g., Ti20Hf20Cu20Ni20Be20 and Ti16.7Zr16.7Nb16.7Cu16.7Ni16.7Be16.7)
papers.approach: Alloy composition modification through similar element substitution/addition to adjust atomic size distribution (and thus lattice distortion) and liquidus temperature
papers.findings: Adjustments in elemental makeup (substitution of Zr with Hf, or addition of Nb) directly affect parameters such as the reduced glass transition temperature and the critical diameter, indicating that fine-tuning composition can improve or degrade glass-forming ability.
papers.mechanism: Variation in lattice distortion (expressed via the δ′ parameter) influences dense atomic packing and affects whether a crystalline or amorphous phase forms, with higher lattice distortion promoting glass formation.

established: Phosphorus addition in high-entropy alloys lowers the liquidus temperature and broadens the solidification range, promoting amorphization under rapid cooling.
High configurational entropy and atomic size mismatch contribute to enhanced glass-forming ability by stabilizing the amorphous state.
Cooling rate is critically linked to the formation of amorphous structures, with faster rates generally suppressing crystallization.

approaches_tried.approach: Variation of cooling rates (from moderate to extremely rapid cooling methods such as melt-spinning)
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved glass formation observed with rapid cooling, though accompanied by shifts in transformation temperatures and potential trade-offs in internal stresses.

approaches_tried.approach: Element substitution/addition (e.g., adding phosphorus, substituting similar elements)
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced amorphous phase formation and modified crystallization behavior; however, potential issues such as reduced ductility have been noted.

approaches_tried.approach: Computational modeling and micro-alloying simulations (using parameters like ΔH, δ, and δ′)
approaches_tried.outcome: Predicted glass-forming ability correlates well with experimental observations, offering a pathway to identify optimal compositions.

mechanisms: Phosphorus reduces the solidification temperature range and favors formation of phosphide phases that disrupt crystalline nucleation.
High mixing entropy increases structural disorder, raising the energy barrier for crystal nucleation and enhancing thermal stability.
Atomic size mismatch increases liquid viscosity, thereby hindering atomic mobility required for crystallization.
disagreements: While phosphorus addition is generally seen to promote amorphization, some evidence suggests that it may also adversely affect ductility and toughness, leading to trade-offs in mechanical properties.
The net benefit of high configurational entropy can vary; in some cases, increased entropy may raise the liquidus temperature which could deteriorate glass-forming ability.
open_questions: What single compositional intervention in phosphorus-rich high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys can simultaneously improve both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state without negatively impacting ductility?
How does the precise phosphorus concentration interact with other elemental constituents to optimize the balance between undercooling effects and the formation of undesirable crystalline phases?
What are the long-term thermal and mechanical behavior implications of such an intervention under varied cooling rate conditions?
opportunities: Investigate targeted variations in phosphorus concentration (or its relative atomic percentage) as a singular compositional modification in high-entropy alloys, while keeping other parameters constant.
Explore systematic coupling of phosphorus adjustment with controlled cooling protocols to finely tune the nucleation kinetics and stabilize the amorphous phase.

Combine the insights from similar element substitution (e.g., tuning lattice distortion via δ′) with phosphorus additions to design alloys with improved glass-forming ability and enhanced thermal stability.
Use computational tools (machine learning and thermodynamic modeling) to predict the optimal intervention conditions in phosphorus-containing systems and validate these predictions experimentally.

directions.assessment: Directly addresses both improved undercooling and delayed crystallization by further reducing the liquidus temperature. Prior studies show that phosphorus addition broadens the solidification range (PMC11642357::web::020::4_discussion) and enhances amorphization. This approach is based on well‐established thermodynamics and is highly feasible.

Uses ultrasonic vibrations to homogenize the melt, ensuring a uniform phosphorus distribution. This may reduce heterogeneous nucleation sites and improve glass‐forming ability without altering the overall composition. Evidence supports homogeneous elemental distributions as beneficial (PMC11480990::web::073::feature_interpretation). The method is experimentally feasible.

A brief thermal treatment below the glass transition temperature would promote structural relaxation and drive phosphorus into local environments that stabilize the amorphous matrix. This single thermal intervention has been used in other MG systems to enhance thermal stability (PMC9023469::web::019::4_discussion) and is experimentally accessible.

directions.direction: Application of an electromagnetic field during quenching
directions.assessment: An applied field during rapid cooling could modify atomic kinetics and influence phosphorus bonding states. Although less common than cooling rate or compositional adjustments, there is emerging evidence on field-assisted solidification affecting nucleation; the approach remains moderately speculative but testable.

Minor addition of elements that preferentially interact with phosphorus (e.g., boron or silicon) may improve the role of P in suppressing crystallization. However, this intervention introduces an extra element and may confound the isolated role of phosphorus, making the mechanism less direct.

candidates.hypothesis: Application of ultrasound during melt processing will promote a more homogeneous distribution of phosphorus in a Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, thereby enhancing its glass-forming ability and increasing the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
candidates.intervention: Incorporate an ultrasonic vibration stage (using frequencies around 20–40 kHz with controlled amplitude) into the melt processing immediately after melting and prior to quenching.

candidates.hypothesis: A brief isothermal annealing treatment below the glass transition temperature (Tg) applied post-solidification will induce structural relaxation and beneficial local redistribution of phosphorus in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy, thereby enhancing thermal stability and glass-forming ability.
candidates.intervention: Subject the as-quenched amorphous alloy to an isothermal anneal at (Tg – 20 K) for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere.

candidates.hypothesis: Applying an external electromagnetic field during the quenching process will alter the atomic kinetics in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy, promoting a bonding state of phosphorus that enhances glass formation and thermal stability.
candidates.intervention: Expose the molten alloy to an external static electromagnetic field (e.g., 0.5–1 Tesla) during the rapid quenching stage.
